questions.q: Raj invests ₹10,000 at 12% annual returns. After 10 years, his investment grows to ₹31,058. After 20 years, it grows to ₹96,463. Why does the second 10 years add ₹65,405 while the first adds only ₹21,058?
options: Returns are higher in later years because the stock market performs better over time
The second 10 years compounds on a larger base, so interest earns interest on more money
Inflation reduces the value of money, so later returns appear larger
The RBI increases interest rates automatically after 10 years
questions.explain: Compounding accelerates over time—interest earned in year 11 is calculated on ₹31,058, not the original ₹10,000, creating exponential growth.

questions.q: During a market crash, Nifty falls 15%. Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) sell ₹5,000 crore of Indian stocks, but Domestic Institutional Investors (DIIs) buy ₹4,000 crore. What is the net likely impact?
options: Nifty will fall further because more money is leaving than entering
Nifty will recover because DIIs buying shows confidence in Indian markets
The ₹1,000 crore difference determines the exact direction Nifty moves next
FII selling pressure dominates since foreign investors control 40% of market cap
questions.explain: DII buying during FII selling is significant—it shows domestic institutions (mutual funds, insurance companies) are supporting the market, which typically stabilizes and can reverse downtrends.

questions.q: Nifty 50 index is at 22,000. Company XYZ's stock price rises 8% while Nifty rises only 3%. What does this tell you?
options: XYZ is a safer investment because it outperformed the index
XYZ has higher risk or is benefiting from sector-specific factors—it's more volatile than the broader market
XYZ will definitely continue outperforming Nifty for the next quarter
The stock market is inefficient and prices are set randomly
questions.explain: When an individual stock significantly outperforms the index, it indicates higher volatility or company-specific catalysts—not safety or guaranteed future returns.

questions.q: Priya invests ₹5,000 monthly via SIP in a mutual fund. In month 1, NAV is ₹100 (50 units). In month 2, NAV drops to ₹80 (62.5 units). In month 3, NAV rises to ₹100 (50 units). How many total units does she own?
options: 150 units—she bought the same amount each month
162.5 units—the SIP bought more units when NAV was low, lowering her average cost
152.5 units—the second month's cheaper NAV offset the third month's gains
Cannot determine without knowing the exact NAV on day 1
questions.explain: SIP's power lies in cost averaging: buying more units when NAV is low (₹80) and fewer when high (₹100) naturally reduces average purchase price below ₹93.

questions.q: The RBI raises interest rates from 6% to 7%. You hold a 10-year Government bond bought at 6%. What happens to its market value?
options: It increases because higher rates make bonds more attractive
It decreases because new bonds now offer 7%, making your 6% bond worth less to a buyer
It stays the same because you hold it until maturity and will get full par value
It increases in value but only if you sell within 6 months
questions.explain: Bond prices move inversely to interest rates—when new bonds offer 7%, nobody wants to buy your 6% bond at par, so its price must fall to compensate the buyer for lower returns.
